blocks.text: My hands would not stop shaking at the Ringing, and still I closed each ring the way I would close one on a young bird's leg: the copper warmed first in my palm, the band laid gently on, the gap pressed shut under my thumb until the ends met. Joan, twenty-three. Mercy, twenty-four. Abel, twenty-five. Rhys, twenty-six. Lucas, twenty-seven. My own, seventy-one, last and one-handed. Then I held out the withy, and Lucas took it from my wrist onto his own without once lifting his eyes to mine.

Across the trestle table Gosmoor Commons' Wing watched my hands. He was a broad man with a white moustache and a stub of chalk behind one ear, and he had flown a hundred matches in the Marsh Circuit. I had flown none.

The four counters stood at the end of the table under the bare ash by the Roost path. The eldest of them put her hand into a felt bag, drew out a brass token and turned it to the light, and wrote on the team sheet in a small square hand: Gosmoor Commons to attack the north-east Roost.
"Only thing in the Fen that leans," Rhys said at my shoulder, "and it leans their way."
"It's the lot," Joan said. "Nobody leaned on it."

"Two hundred years of record books, Crate." Rhys was speaking to me, because I was the one who did not know to stop him. "North-east Roosts score more than they ought. The Courier calls it the Northing and prints a little arrow by the fixtures. I've always thought the arrow should be me, pointing."
"You'll stop talking about arrows now, won't you, and go and stand by your decoys?" Joan said.
"Any sighted players to declare?" the eldest counter asked.
Nobody spoke. Lucas had his hand flat on the table, the one with the fine burn scar across the back of it, and he was looking down at it as if it belonged to somebody else.

It was the second Saturday of my life on Hobsmere Reedbed, and the first on which I stood inside the reed-line. The wind was light out of the south-west, hardly enough to stir the tassels on the reed, and the mere lay behind the north-east Roost the colour of pewter, very flat, with a skin of ice along the margin where the coots had given up and stood in rows on it. There were lapwings up over the far grazing, tumbling and calling, and a single heron going home low over the water with its legs trailing like a dropped thought. The crowd along the causeway bank was thinner than the week before. People do not walk far in the cold to watch the bottom club lose.
Joan came to me at the reed-line with Mercy beside her.

"We keep your shades down until five past four," she said. "No flock goes into a Roost before roost-light, so there's nothing to win in High Flight. You raise at five past, you take your Breath when they call it, you fly to full dark. That's twenty-four minutes. Fourteen to walk down. You'll do it that way, won't you?"
"Fourteen minutes," I said, and looked at Lucas, standing alone halfway to Gosmoor's Roost with the withy pale on his wrist.
"Fourteen," Joan said, and did not look at him.

The Loft men brought the crate out to centre on its poles. It was a Mallow crate, the paint gone soft at the corners where my own hands had lifted it a hundred times, and I knew before the slats came up how the birds inside would be sitting: close and drowsy, shoulders together, because Mallow were always the first flock at the Loft to want their perches when the light began to go. At twenty to four the counters dropped their hands and the slats came up, and the Loose went into the grey air like a handful of seed thrown at the sky, scattered, then gathered, then turning all together over the reed as if one bird had remembered for all of them which way was up.

Gosmoor's Wing raised at once. I saw his six shades come up over his runners, dark and steady, flying at a ceiling just above the flock's middle, and within the minute there was another shape among them, and I counted it before I could stop myself.

The forty-first bird came in at the north-east edge of the flock, over no runner, low and unhurried, and stayed there. It did not drift along the edge the way an ordinary bird does when the flock turns. Wherever the Mallow birds went, it kept to the side of them that faced the mere, and the flock, all the while, sat a little north-east of where it should have been, the way a field of reed leans when the wind has gone out of it and the reed still remembers. I watched it for a long time. It looked to me as if it were leaning on them.
I kept my hands at my sides until five past four, as Joan had said, and watched Gosmoor's herding walk the Mallow flock steadily toward the end we had to defend.
At five past four I called my shades.

They came up over my crew like six dark kites on one string, and for a moment, seeing them there, ours and real and answering me, I forgot to be afraid. I set them at the flock's height and sent Joan and Mercy wide along the south edge, Rhys and Abel under the leading birds, and I felt the edge of the flock bend toward us, a little, the way a curtain bends toward an open window.
Then Gosmoor's Wing brought his ceiling to mine.

I saw it happen. His six shades slid down through the air until they were flying at my height exactly, and every bird at the edge of the flock now had one of mine and one of his among its seven, and the two cancelled each other like hands pressed palm to palm. I lifted my ceiling. My shades lagged, the whole of a breath, rising slowly and loosely the way gulls rise off water, and before they had settled his were beside them again. I dropped it. He followed. He did not hurry. He only ever arrived a breath after me, and a breath was all he needed.

I wanted the flock to answer me. I had wanted it all week, at night in Joan's back bedroom with the wind in the thatch, and on the training ground at Pollard's roost, and now it was forty birds above me in the last grey light and it would not. Shade for shade, he took my herding apart. By ten past four the Mallow flock was over the north-east half of the Reedbed with the mere shining beyond it, and at eleven minutes past the eldest counter lifted her flag and called roost-light.
"Forty of forty," she said. "Counted flock forty."
Above the north-east edge the forty-first bird flew on beside them, and I said nothing.

The Gloaming came in from the east as it always does on the levels, the dark rising off the grazing before it falls from the sky, so that for a while the ground is night and the air is still day. Gosmoor's Tackers ran their decoys out to our Roost and planted them by its mouth, two wooden starlings on reed-poles, lower than a man's head. Their Callers spread wide. Their Wing kept his ceiling on mine and his herding at the flock's edge, patient as a drain filling.
I could not push the forty. Pollard had told me so. So I tried to hold one.

I signalled the Callers and the crew came in under the point bird, all six of us, close enough to touch: Joan's shoulder at my left and Rhys at my right, Abel and Mercy behind, Lucas with his hand almost on my sleeve. Our six shades closed round one bird at the flock's leading edge, ahead and behind and either side, so near it that I could see its threads running to them, six bright lines to six of ours, and only one left over to its own kind.

It turned. I watched it turn, a small brown starling with the last light under its wing, coming round toward the south-west and the Roost we were attacking, and for three wingbeats it was ours. But the flock was not leaning that way. The flock was leaning north-east, toward the mere and the forty-first bird and the decoys Gosmoor had planted by our Roost, and the birds around my bird felt it go and simply went on without it, and it slid back among them as if it had never left. Six can turn a bird. Six cannot hold one. Somewhere in Wenlode, that night, a clerk would enter our shape in the flight book against the Mallow flock as spent, and it had bought us nothing.
"Breath," the eldest counter called. "Twenty minutes, Hobsmere. Breath."
I dropped every shade. It was twenty-five past four.

It is a long minute, the Breath, when you have only just learned what your shades feel like. My arms were empty. Above me Gosmoor's six worked the flock without anyone to answer them, and the main body of the Mallow birds poured toward the north-east Roost in a long, dark, falling sheet, and Joan beside me said something about back-flow that I did not hear.

But I was still reading, because reading costs nothing. I followed seven birds' threads at a time, as many as I can ever follow, and I saw that the flock was not one flock any more. The dark had come into the middle of it. The birds on the south-west side, the trailing birds, had stopped counting the north-east birds among their seven. Their threads ran only to one another now, a loose lobe of them hanging back over the reed, and their point bird was dropping, and dropping, the way Mallow birds always dropped toward their perches when the light went, wanting down.
They wanted down. They did not mind where.
"Lucas," I said. "Their Roost. Now."

He went. He ran the way a clockmaker might run, very upright, very exact, through the reed toward the south-west Roost, where Rhys and Abel had already planted our decoys low beside the mouth. The counter's hand came down. The Breath was over.

Joan and Mercy and I ran in under the trailing lobe. I called my ceiling down almost to the thatch and raised all six, and they came up lagging, settling low: Lucas's shade over the doorway of Gosmoor's Roost, Rhys's and Abel's beside the decoys, and Joan's and Mercy's and mine coming in behind the falling birds as we ran. I did not try to turn the trailing lobe against anything. I only gave its falling point bird somewhere to fall. It was already leaning that way. The grain was with us. The point bird went down to Lucas's shade like a leaf to water and the lobe went down behind it, and I watched them go in under the thatch in a soft, dark, rushing pour, wings closing, one after another after another.
At the other end Gosmoor's main body went down into our Roost the same way.

At half past four the eldest counter called full dark. My shades fell. And in the last of the light, as the Roosts went quiet, I saw the forty-first bird leave the flock it had leaned on all evening and go out low and straight across Hobsmere Mere, a little darker than the water, until I could not tell it from the dark.
The counters went to the Roosts with their lanterns. Twenty in the south-west Roost, for us. Twenty in the north-east, for Gosmoor.
"Half and half," the eldest counter said, and wrote it. "Partial settle each. Two each."
Joan stood with her hands on her knees for a moment. Then she straightened and said, quite quietly, "Eleven points. Still bottom. Still breathing."

The counters cut our rings at the reed-line. I held out my wrist and watched the snips go through the copper, and I was sorry to feel it go, which I had not expected. The withy stayed on Lucas. Behind us the Loft men were crating the Mallow birds out of both Roosts by lantern light, and a boy I did not know was lifting them, the way I had lifted them, into the crate I had carried a hundred times. I wanted very much to go and show him how Mallow like to be held, low against the chest. I did not.

The Dyke Arms stands at the Reedbed end of the causeway with its back to the mere, and after a home match the counters write up their sheet at the table in its back room, with both Wings to sign. Joan sat me down by the window and said Lucas would walk me down the moment my name was on it, wouldn't he, and Lucas sat on the bench beside me with the withy on his wrist, not touching me yet. I could feel the pull already, but it lay only toward the yard behind the inn wall where the crates were, the way a dog lies toward a door. Gosmoor's Wing signed and shook my hand and said I had good eyes. I signed under him, and the eldest counter began to blot the sheet.

Rhys came in last. The landlord handed him an envelope from behind the bar, and I saw its edge as it passed under the lamp, grey and gold, Fallowby Wardens' colours. I knew them from the draw board at the Loft, where every club's fixture card hangs on a ribbon of its own colour. Rhys opened it, read it once, and put it inside his coat.
"Who writes to you?" Mercy asked.
"Admirers," Rhys said. "Have any of you looked at my hair since the Roost? I went under a decoy pole at full stretch. I think I've a reed in it. Crate, have I a reed in it?"
He bent his head to me, and I looked, because he had asked.
"No," I said. "It's all right."

"All right," Rhys said. "She says all right. To this." But he did not look at me while he said it, and his hand stayed flat on his coat, over the letter, until Joan asked him whether he would be buying a round or only describing one.
Outside, Wilfred Cobbing's eel-cart went creaking over the causeway with the crates roped on behind, and on the far side, on the Wenlode road, the Loft van's lamps came on.

It began the way the tide begins on a flat shore, so slowly that I did not feel it begin, only that it had. The direction in me lifted off the inn wall and swung, steadily, out across the dark, and settled on a line I could have drawn with a ruler: from my chest, through the window, over the reed, over Hobsmere Mere, toward the van on the Wenlode road and the Mallow birds in their crate, going home to the Circuit Loft.
The line went straight across the water. It went across Hamish's water.
Lucas was already standing. He took my hand.
"Fourteen," he said. "We'll do it outside. You'll w-want to walk."

I did want to. We went out of the inn into the cold, and he walked beside me down through the trodden reed toward the mere, and each time my feet tried to take me straight he turned me gently along the shore instead, and talked. He talked about clocks. He told me how an escapement works, how it holds the whole weight of a wheel back and lets it go one tooth at a time, one tooth, and holds, and one tooth, and how a clock is nothing but a thing that has been taught to let go slowly. His voice was very even. He counted the minutes aloud, one at each tooth, and I let him count them.
"Six," he said. "Seven. That's half. You're doing w-well."
At eight his voice changed.

He had stopped looking at me. He was looking out across the mere, the same way I was looking, straight along my line toward the far bank and the faint lamps of the van, and I felt his fingers tighten round mine, and then I felt them begin to shake. It was a small shake at first, the kind you feel in a bird's legs when you lift it from the crate and it has not yet decided whether to trust you. Then it was not small.
"Lucas," I said.
"Nine," he said, but not to me.

The mere was very black. There was no moon yet, only the far, thin lamps across the water and the reed standing grey and still to either side of us, every stem with its own small edge of frost, and the ice at the margin lay pale as a cut loaf, and beyond it the open water did not move at all, and I could hear it anyway, the soft, deep, patient sound that cold water makes against ice in the dark when nothing else is making any sound. I could smell it. I could smell the mud under the reed and the snow that had not come yet and the old smoke of the inn behind us, and I held on to each of these as I named it, the reed, the ice, the black water, the far lamps, as if naming them would keep them where they were and keep me where I was. A coot called once out on the water and was quiet. The line in my chest ran straight past it. Lucas's hand shook so hard now that it was my hand holding his.
Then it was nobody's.

Lucas's grip failed, his fingers opening out of mine like a gate swinging on its hinge, and I went on alone down the frozen reed toward Hobsmere Mere, on the line Hamish had walked a week before, toward the black water where at full dark I had watched the forty-first bird go out low across it and not come back.
